content.page_title: Anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapy in PCI/ACS (excerpt)
content.summary: Discussion of P2Y12 receptor inhibition (specifically cangrelor) in the setting of PCI for CCS and ACS, and recommendations for anticoagulant treatment in the acute phase of ACS including avoidance of crossover between anticoagulants and use of parenteral anticoagulation at diagnosis.
key_points: Cangrelor is a direct, reversible, short-acting P2Y12 receptor inhibitor evaluated during PCI for CCS and ACS in trials versus clopidogrel (CHAMPION trials).
Meta-analysis showed benefit of cangrelor for ischaemic endpoints was counterbalanced by increased minor bleeding; benefit attenuated with upfront clopidogrel.

Cangrelor may be considered on a case-by-case basis in P2Y12 receptor inhibitor–naïve ACS patients undergoing PCI, including patients who cannot take oral drugs (e.g., cardiogenic shock or mechanical ventilation).
Anticoagulation is recommended for all ACS patients at diagnosis; parenteral anticoagulation preferred when invasive strategy used.
Avoid crossover between unfractionated heparin (UFH) and low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) except specific scenarios (e.g., adding UFH to fondaparinux when proceeding to PCI).
Anticoagulants generally discontinued immediately after PCI except in specific settings (e.g., LV aneurysm with thrombus formation or AF requiring anticoagulation).
